notes.meaning: Nebuchadnezzar brought a massive army made up of soldiers from many nations to attack Jerusalem and the towns around it. In the middle of this terrifying siege, the Lord spoke directly to Jeremiah.
God sent Jeremiah with a message for King Zedekiah of Judah. The Lord declared that He was handing Jerusalem over to the king of Babylon, who would burn it to the ground.
Zedekiah was warned that he could not run away or escape Babylon's grasp. He would be brought directly before Nebuchadnezzar to hear his sentence face to face, and then be dragged into exile.
God offered Zedekiah a small mercy in the middle of this severe judgment. Even though he would be taken prisoner, he would not be executed or killed by the sword in battle.
Zedekiah would die a natural, peaceful death rather than a violent one. The people would burn sweet-smelling spices in his memory and mourn for him as a king, because the Lord had promised it.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary notes that Zedekiah remained a prisoner in Babylon until death, where the Jewish exiles were allowed to give him an honorable burial.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah faithfully told King Zedekiah every word the Lord had spoken. Delivering such harsh news to a reigning king placed the prophet in grave personal danger, but he carried out his duty.
The Babylonian army was attacking Jerusalem and the only two other fortified cities still holding out in Judah, Lachish and Azekah. All the other towns across the country had already been captured.
King Zedekiah made a covenant—a sacred, binding promise—with the people in Jerusalem to proclaim freedom for their slaves. After this agreement was made, God gave Jeremiah another message.
The covenant required every master to free their Hebrew slaves, both men and women. God's law forbade Israelites from holding their own brothers and sisters in lifelong bondage.
All the leaders and the rest of the people agreed to the covenant and released their bondservants. At first, they obeyed the law and let them go free.
Soon after granting freedom, the slave owners changed their minds. When the Babylonian siege temporarily stopped, they forced their former servants back into slavery.
The Lord spoke again to Jeremiah to confront the nation for breaking their promise. God holds His people accountable when they act unjustly toward others.
God reminded them of the covenant He made with their ancestors after rescuing them from slavery in Egypt. Because the Lord had set them free, they were never supposed to oppress their own people.

God's law commanded that any Hebrew servant could work for only six years and had to be released in the seventh year. However, earlier generations had ignored God's voice and refused to obey this command.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some popular teachers see the six years of servitude followed by release in the seventh year as a symbol of humanity suffering under Satan for six thousand years before finding freedom in Christ's thousand-year reign.

notes.meaning: Zedekiah and the people had recently done what was right by releasing their neighbors from slavery. They had even made a formal vow before God in the temple that honored His name.

By dragging the freed servants back into bondage, the masters broke their oath and dishonored God's holy name. They treated their vow to God as meaningless and used force to strip their brothers of their freedom.

Because the masters refused to grant true freedom to their brothers, God declared that He would set them 'free' to face war, disease, and starvation. He withdrew His protection, leaving them exposed to terror and scattering them across the earth.

When they made their vow, the people had cut a young calf in half and walked between the pieces, silently asking to be cut apart if they broke their word. Because they violated the covenant, God declared He would tear them apart just like that animal.

All levels of society had participated in this sacred ritual, from princes and royal palace officials to priests and ordinary citizens. Because all of them had walked between the pieces of the calf, none of them were exempt from God's judgment.

God promised to hand these covenant-breakers over to ruthless enemies who wanted them dead. Their bodies would not receive an honorable burial, but would be left on the ground for birds and wild beasts to eat.
King Zedekiah and his rulers would be handed over to the Babylonian army that had temporarily marched away. The people thought the danger had passed, but their relief was only an illusion.

The Lord announced that He would summon the Babylonians back to Jerusalem under His command. They would besiege the city, take it, set it on fire, and leave the towns of Judah completely ruined and empty.
